original_question: Find an exact formula for the number of lozenge tilings of the hexagon with side lengths n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 after deleting the central triangle.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2 ('Lozenges'): 'Enumerate the lozenge tilings of the region obtained from the n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 hexagon by removing the central triangle.' ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's intended target very closely: it asks for an exact enumeration of lozenge tilings of the alternating-side hexagon n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 after removal of the central triangle, which is exactly the content of Problem 2. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
missing_details: The paper is working on the triangular lattice: a lozenge is a unit rhombus with angles 60° and 120°, and the region is tiled by such lozenges. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))

The hexagon should be specified as having integer side lengths n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 in cyclic order, with all internal angles equal to 120°. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
The parameter should be quantified explicitly: the problem is to determine the count for each positive integer n. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))

The removed object is the central unit equilateral triangle; saying only 'central triangle' leaves its lattice size implicit. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))

For a fully stand-alone formulation, it helps to note the hidden motivation from the nearby context: the undeleted hexagon is not lozenge-tileable because its numbers of upward- and downward-pointing unit triangles differ, and deleting the central triangle restores tileability. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))

No ambient ring/field, operator definitions, homogeneity assumptions, degree restrictions, nilpotency conditions, or 'sufficiently large' quantifiers are part of the paper's statement; those notions are inapplicable here because this is a finite enumerative tiling problem. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
refined_question: For each positive integer n, let H_n be the hexagon in the triangular lattice with internal angles 120° and side lengths n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 in cyclic order. Remove the central unit equilateral triangle from H_n. Determine exactly the number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region, where a lozenge is a unit rhombus formed by two adjacent unit triangles. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, determine the number of perfect matchings of the finite honeycomb graph dual to the dissection of that punctured hexagon into unit triangles. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 2, not a broader neighboring statement: the side-length pattern and the deletion of the central triangle coincide exactly with the official problem on p. 8. The paragraph immediately before Problem 2 supplies the key hidden assumption that the original n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 hexagon is not tileable until the central triangle is removed. Section 2 also gives the ambient geometric conventions needed to make the question self-contained: lozenges are unit rhombi, the regions live on the triangular lattice, and semiregular hexagons are specified by side lengths in cyclic order. I therefore sharpened the draft only by making those implicit conventions explicit and by adding the universal quantifier 'for each positive integer n'; I did not broaden the problem to the later progress-note generalizations (a, b+1, b, a+1, b, b+1) or (a, b+1, c, a+1, b, c+1), because your draft clearly points to the special case singled out as Problem 2. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))
